title: Marked-root Weyl presentations are connected through rank-two parabolics
statement:
Let $(M,\Phi,M^\vee,\Phi^\vee,\Delta)$ be a finite reduced based root datum with the meaning of [def-sfb-pinned-split-root-realization]; no group scheme is assumed. Put $s_a(m)=m-\langle m,a^\vee\rangle a$ and let $W$ be the subgroup of automorphisms of $M$ generated by $s_a$ for $a\in\Delta$. Products act on roots from right to left. For distinct $a,b\in\Delta$, write $W_{ab}=\langle s_a,s_b\rangle$ and $\Phi_{ab}^+=\Phi\cap(\mathbf Z_{\geq0}a+\mathbf Z_{\geq0}b)$. On $W\times\Delta$ let $\sim$ be the smallest equivalence relation containing
$$(w,c)\sim(wv,e)\quad\text{if }a\ne b,\ c,e\in\{a,b\},\ v\in W_{ab},\ v(e)=c.$$
The map $(w,c)\mapsto w(c)$ is onto $\Phi$, and two pairs have the same image if and only if they are equivalent under $\sim$.

Moreover, for every distinct $a,b$, every $e\in\{a,b\}$, and every $v\in W_{ab}$ with $v(e)\in\Phi_{ab}^+$, there exist $j_1,\ldots,j_k\in\{a,b\}$ such that $v=s_{j_k}\cdots s_{j_1}$ and
$$e_i=s_{j_i}\cdots s_{j_1}(e)\in\Phi_{ab}^+\quad(0\leq i\leq k),\qquad e_0=e.$$
In particular $e_{i-1}\ne j_i$ for each $i\geq1$. Every $c\in\Phi_{ab}^+$ is $v(e)$ for some such $e,v$. Empty root data, rank one, reducible root data, and a central lattice complementary to the root span are permitted.

proof.text: By [lem-sfb-based-root-datum-coxeter-presentation], the group generated by all root reflections is finite and equals the simple-reflection group $W$ in the statement. Work on $L=M\otimes_{\mathbf Z}\mathbf R$ and $E=\operatorname{span}_{\mathbf R}\Phi$. Average any positive definite form $B_0$ on $L$ to obtain $B(x,y)=\sum_{w\in W}B_0(wx,wy)$. It is positive definite and $W$-invariant: each nonzero $x$ has $B(x,x)>0$, and multiplication permutes the summands. Each $s_r$ has $-1$-eigenspace $\mathbf Rr$ and fixes $\ker\langle -,r^\vee\rangle$; invariance makes these eigenspaces orthogonal. Thus $\langle x,r^\vee\rangle=2B(x,r)/B(r,r)$, so all reflections are the orthogonal root reflections. They fix $E^\perp$ pointwise. Consequently restriction to $E$ is faithful, including in the presence of a central lattice, and identifies $W$ with the full root reflection group of $\Phi\subset E$.

source.place: Conrad Theorem 6.2.4 proof, printed p.202, omitted Tits compatibility; agent chamber argument using Milne Appendix C.8--C.22.

proof.text: The root datum axioms make $\Phi\subset E$ a finite reduced spanning crystallographic real root system: the orthogonal formula in step 1 supplies integrality, and rational coordinates show real proportionality of roots is rational proportionality. The given $\Delta$ is a real basis of $E$ with the required same-sign integral expansions. Apply [lem-sfb-root-chamber-simple-transitivity]. Write $C=\{x:B(x,d)>0\ (d\in\Delta)\}$ and $H_r=\{x:B(x,r)=0\}$. Every chamber is uniquely $wC$, with positive roots $w\Phi^+$ and inward facet roots $w\Delta$. Indeed, its closure is the cone $B(x,wd)\geq0$ in the independent coordinate functions indexed by $d\in\Delta$, so its facets are exactly their individual zero sets. If $\Phi=\varnothing$, the domain $W\times\Delta$ and codomain are empty and all conclusions are vacuous; assume henceforth $\Phi\ne\varnothing$.

source.place: Conrad Theorem 6.2.4 proof, printed p.202, omitted Tits compatibility; agent chamber argument using Milne Appendix C.8--C.22.

proof.text: Fix $\gamma\in\Phi$. On $H_\gamma$, take the finite arrangement consisting of the distinct proper hyperplanes $H_\gamma\cap H_r$ for $r\ne\pm\gamma$. They are proper because the reduced root system has no other root on $\mathbf R\gamma$. The density assertion of [lem-sfb-arrangement-generic-broken-line] supplies $x$ on none of them, also when $H_\gamma=0$. For small $\epsilon>0$, the points near $x+\epsilon\gamma$ have the same nonzero signs on all $r\ne\pm\gamma$ as $x$, and positive pairing with $\gamma$. They form the chamber on that side of $H_\gamma$ near $x$. Its closure contains a relatively open neighbourhood of $x$ in $H_\gamma$, so this is a facet. By step 2 the chamber is $wC$ and its unique inward root on this facet is $w(c)$ for some $c\in\Delta$. Reducedness and the positive orientation give $w(c)=\gamma$. This proves surjectivity.

source.place: Conrad Theorem 6.2.4 proof, printed p.202, omitted Tits compatibility; agent chamber argument using Milne Appendix C.8--C.22.

proof.text: Each generating identification preserves the root: $wv(e)=w(c)$. Equality of root images is itself an equivalence relation, so it contains the generated relation $\sim$. It remains to connect any two pairs with common image $\gamma$.

source.place: Conrad Theorem 6.2.4 proof, printed p.202, omitted Tits compatibility; agent chamber argument using Milne Appendix C.8--C.22.

proof.text: For this $\gamma$, use the restricted arrangement on $H_\gamma$ from step 3. Each of its regular points $x$ determines a unique chamber on the $\gamma$-positive side, by the signs at $x+\epsilon\gamma$ for small $\epsilon>0$. On each restricted component those signs are constant, since a continuous nonzero real function has constant sign on a connected set. Conversely a fixed sign region is an intersection of strict linear half-spaces, hence convex and connected. Thus restricted components correspond exactly to chambers with an inward $\gamma$-facet. For a pair $(w,c)$ with $w(c)=\gamma$, choose the point on that facet with $B(x,wd)=1$ for $d\ne c$ and $B(x,wc)=0$. A root vanishes there only when its expansion in $w\Delta$ is supported at $c$, hence only for $\pm\gamma$. It is therefore a regular restricted point. This identifies $(w,c)$ with the corresponding restricted component; the chamber determines $w$ uniquely by step 2, and then $c$ uniquely.

source.place: Conrad Theorem 6.2.4 proof, printed p.202, omitted Tits compatibility; agent chamber argument using Milne Appendix C.8--C.22.

proof.text: For $(w,c)$ and $(u,d)$ with image $\gamma$, choose their restricted regular points as in step 5. Apply [lem-sfb-arrangement-generic-broken-line] on the real vector space $H_\gamma$, with $U=H_\gamma$, to join them by a finite sequence of restricted components crossing one restricted hyperplane at a time. If its dimension is zero, there are no crossings and step 5 already identifies the pairs. At any crossing point $q$, let $K$ be the unique restricted hyperplane met. All roots vanishing at $q$ have ambient hyperplanes containing $K$: any other restricted hyperplane through $q$ would violate the generic-path assertion. Conversely every ambient root hyperplane containing $K$ vanishes there. Their normals span exactly the two-dimensional space $K^\perp\subset E$, since $H_\gamma$ and at least one other ambient hyperplane intersect in $K$.

source.place: Conrad Theorem 6.2.4 proof, printed p.202, omitted Tits compatibility; agent chamber argument using Milne Appendix C.8--C.22.

proof.text: Let $w_iC,w_{i+1}C$ be the chambers on the $\gamma$-positive side before and after such a crossing. Both closures contain $q$. Put $J=\{j\in\Delta:B(w_i^{-1}q,j)=0\}$. All other simple pairings are positive. By [lem-sfb-chamber-face-parabolic-residue] the roots vanishing at $w_i^{-1}q$ span $\operatorname{span}J$, so step 6 forces $J=\{a,b\}$ with $a\ne b$. The same node gives $w_i^{-1}w_{i+1}C=vC$ for some $v\in W_{ab}$. Freeness from [lem-sfb-root-chamber-simple-transitivity] makes $w_{i+1}=w_iv$. The marked roots $c_i,c_{i+1}$ belong to $\{a,b\}$: their facets contain $q$, and for $c_{i+1}$ this also uses that $v$ fixes $w_i^{-1}q$. Their inward orientations give $w_i(c_i)=\gamma=w_iv(c_{i+1})$, hence $v(c_{i+1})=c_i$. This is precisely one of the specified generating identifications. The finite chain connects the original pairs. Together with step 4 this proves the equivalence assertion.

source.place: Conrad Theorem 6.2.4 proof, printed p.202, omitted Tits compatibility; agent chamber argument using Milne Appendix C.8--C.22.

proof.text: Fix distinct $a,b\in\Delta$. In $E_{ab}=\mathbf Ra+\mathbf Rb$ put $R_{ab}=\Phi\cap E_{ab}$. This is a reduced spanning crystallographic root system, because reflections in its roots preserve both this plane and the full root set. The base is $\{a,b\}$: the $\Delta$-coordinates of every root in the plane vanish outside $a,b$, and hence its remaining integral coordinates have one sign. Its positive roots are exactly $\Phi_{ab}^+$. Apply [lem-sfb-simple-root-reflection-generation] to identify its full reflection group with $W_{ab}$ on the plane; restriction is faithful since $s_a,s_b$ fix the orthogonal complement pointwise. Apply [lem-sfb-root-chamber-simple-transitivity] to this plane and write $C_{ab}=\{x:B(x,a)>0,B(x,b)>0\}$.

source.place: Conrad Theorem 6.2.4 proof, printed p.202, omitted Tits compatibility; agent chamber argument using Milne Appendix C.8--C.22.

proof.text: Let $e\in\{a,b\}$ and $v(e)\in\Phi_{ab}^+$. Both $C_{ab}$ and $v^{-1}C_{ab}$ lie in the open half-plane $U=\{x:B(x,e)>0\}$: for $y=v^{-1}x$ the pairing is $B(y,e)=B(x,v(e))>0$. Choose regular points in those chambers and apply [lem-sfb-arrangement-generic-broken-line] to the finite root-line arrangement in $E_{ab}$ and this convex open $U$. The resulting gallery remains in $U$. Label its chambers $t_iC_{ab}$, starting $t_0=1$ and ending $t_k=v^{-1}$, using [lem-sfb-root-chamber-simple-transitivity]. At a crossing there is just one vanishing root line. In the coordinates of $t_{i-1}C_{ab}$ the zero set of simple roots therefore has size one. By [lem-sfb-chamber-face-parabolic-residue] and freeness, $t_i=t_{i-1}s_{j_i}$ for some $j_i\in\{a,b\}$. Thus $t_i^{-1}=s_{j_i}\cdots s_{j_1}$ and $v=s_{j_k}\cdots s_{j_1}$. Since $t_iC_{ab}\subset U$, the root $t_i^{-1}e$ is positive by the positive-root formula in the chamber theorem. These are exactly the required $e_i$.

source.place: Conrad Theorem 6.2.4 proof, printed p.202, omitted Tits compatibility; agent chamber argument using Milne Appendix C.8--C.22.

proof.text: If $e_{i-1}=j_i$, then $e_i=s_{j_i}(j_i)=-j_i$, contradicting its positivity. Finally repeat step 3 inside the plane root system of step 8 for any $c\in\Phi_{ab}^+$; it produces $e\in\{a,b\}$ and $v\in W_{ab}$ with $v(e)=c$. Step 9 applies to that $v$. No irreducibility was used; when the total rank is one there are only the two chambers and the restricted wall is zero-dimensional, so steps 3--7 apply without any rank-two crossing. The empty case was settled in step 2, and step 1 handles the central lattice.
